articles.text: Anna Brown is the former City Clerk of Union City On Monday, October 16, the Piedmont City Council appointed Anna M. Brown as Piedmont’s new City Clerk. Brown comes to Piedmont during a career in local government, most recently as City Clerk in Union City since 2014. Prior to that she served as Deputy City Clerk of South San Francisco for five years. Brown is a Certified Municipal Clerk, a Notary Public, with a Bachelor of Arts degree in Public Administration. On July 17, following the departure of John Tulloch as City Clerk, the council appointed Sheri Hartz as interim city clerk while the city searched for a permanent replacement. The recruiting firm Bob Murray & Associates was hired to initiate a professional search. Over the next six weeks, 25 applicants were considered and six were interviewed. A panel of current and former city clerks was convened to rank the candidates. The panel included Mark Numainville, Berkeley City Clerk, Joanne Robbins, Lafayette City Clerk, and former Piedmont City Clerk John Tulloch. Additional interviews were conducted by some members of the city government, including City Council members and City Administrator Roseanna Bayon Moore. “I am honored and excited to serve the city of Piedmont as its next city clerk,” said Brown. “It is my sincere hope that the work that I do here helps foster a greater sense of trust between the city’s residents and their city government.” The posted salary is $177,000 annually with an auto allowance and health benefits. articles.text: The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade will take place on Saturday, October 28, starting at 11:00 a.m. in front of Pet Food Express at the corner of Montel Avenue. Piedmont Grocery owner Dave Larson will be leading the parade as Grand Marshal in one of his many costumes. Merchants on the street founded the parade in 1986 as a way to celebrate Halloween safely. It has evolved into a highly anticipated community celebration that unites the neighborhood. The street will be closed to vehicles from 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. from Yosemite Avenue to the Piedmont Theater at Linda Avenue. Kids can start stocking up on candy two days before Halloween by trick or treating along the Avenue at participating merchants’ shops. Live music, haunted houses, face painting, and skull craft will have everyone in high Halloween spirit. Free cartoons will be shown for children at the Piedmont Theater starting at 9:45 a.m., and Piedmont Avenue will be packed with kids and adults in costumes on Saturday, October 28, for the 36th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade.

articles.text: Annual event encourages earthquake safety, preparedness Piedmont Fire Department encourages residents to stop what they’re doing this Thursday, October 19 at 10:19 AM and take a few minutes to practice what they would do during an earthquake as part of the annual Great California ShakeOut. Held annually on the third Thursday of October, International Shakeout Day challenges people across the globe to become better prepared to protect themselves in case of an earthquake. More than 9.6 million people in California have signed up to participate in this year’s ShakeOut. The Piedmont Fire Department offers the following advice: Anytime you feel shaking or get an earthquake alert, take these three steps immediately if you are able: 1. DROP to your hands and knees: This position protects you from being knocked down by shaking and reduces your chance of being hit by falling or flying objects. 2. Take COVER under a sturdy desk or table: Stay on your knees and bend over to protect vital organs while covering your head and neck with one arm. If there’s nothing available nearby to shelter under, crawl next to an interior wall. 3. HOLD ON until shaking stops: If you’re sheltering under furniture, hold onto it with one hand and be ready to move with your shelter if it shifts. Otherwise, hold onto your head and neck with both arms and hands. For those in a wheelchair or using a walker: For 25 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. Analysts at the United States Geological Survey (USGS) predict that a major earthquake event of magnitude 6.7 or greater is likely to affect the San Francisco Bay Area before 2032. The Loma Prieta Earthquake of 1989 was measured at 6.9 on the Richter scale, lasted just 15 seconds and caused more than $5 billion in property damage. After practicing “drop, cover, and hold on,” the Fire Department recommends signing up for AC Alert emergency notifications, building or refreshing your disaster supply kit, and making a plan for how you will contact your loved ones after an emergency. articles.text: The first Black family to live in Piedmont, the Dearing family, moved into their home at 67 Wildwood Avenue in early 1924. Within months, a mob of 500 people surrounded their house, demanding they leave because of the color of their skin. That history and more will be shared by Piedmont High School students on Monday, October 23 in a presentation supported by the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC). The event is open to the public and will include light refreshments after the program. History of Piedmont: Racism and Redlining will incorporate a conversation about the history of Piedmont, including the early origins of redlining in the Bay Area and how it affected the Dearing family in particular. Created by members of Piedmont High School’s Associated Student Body, the presentation also follows Piedmont’s complicated legacy in the hopes that it will inspire change and promote an inclusive environment. “The more we know about our past, the better we can aid the future of Piedmont,” said PHS senior Hailey Marshburn, one of the organizers. The presentation will be given to PHS sophomores and juniors in early November. The presentation will take place at 6:30 p.m. on Monday, October 23 in the Alan Harvey Theater, 800 Magnolia Avenue, begin. We also invite you to stay after the program for light refreshments and conversation from 7:30 to 8:30 pm. “A few members of PADC had a chance to see this presentation last year. We were so inspired by it that we wanted everyone in our community to have an opportunity to experience it. The student presentation was well researched, powerful, and is moving.” said Ellen Lee, PADC President. For more information, contact Lee at hiellenlee@gmail.com.

articles.text: Taurid Meteor Shower as seen from Chabot Space and Science Center in the Oakland hills. When the night sky is stretched above us, there is so much to see – even in the dark. Sometimes the dark gives the perfect stage for a special show you would not be able to see clearly in the daytime. A few notso-small examples are the moon and the stars. However, in early November an even more exciting show is coming to the night sky: the Taurid meteor shower. What is a meteor shower? Meteor showers happen when the Earth passes through left over stuff like rocks from asteroids and comets. When these rocks enter the Earth’s atmosphere the air around them gets very hot. So, from Earth the rocks look like bright streaks of light across the sky. If you have ever seen a shooting star, then you know exactly what to look for. During the Taurid meteor shower, the Earth is passing through a comet named Encke. Encke is a small comet that takes 3.3 years to travel around the sun, the shortest travel time of any known comet in our solar system. Why is it called the Taurid Meteor Shower? Meteor showers get their names from the constellations that the meteors seem to be coming from. Constellations are a group of stars that sometimes look like the shapes of objects, animals, or people. For this shower, the meteors are coming from the direction of a constellation called Taurus, a group of stars that look like a bull, so it is called the Taurid meteor shower. When and where can I see it? The Taurid meteor shower is a meteor shower that happens in two parts: the Southern Taurids and the Northern Taurids. These showers begin mid-October and go on up to early December. It is believed that you will be able to see the Northern Taurid stream best between November 12 and 13 and the Southern Taurid stream around November 6. Just like a movie is best to watch in a dark theater, you want to make sure you are in the darkest possible place outside to see this meteor shower. This means you will want to be away from places like cities where all the lights make it more difficult to see the night sky entirely. A one-of-a-kind show There are so many interesting things in the night sky to see and learn about. The Taurid meteor shower is just one of the many examples of why sometimes the best show of all is right above our heads. Cameron Schneider is with Chabot Space & Science Center, a non-profit institution, community resource, and hub for interactive STEAM engagement in Oakland. Founded in 1883, Chabot’s mission is to inspire and educate learners of all ages about the universe and planet Earth.
articles.title: Coming to a night sky near you – the Taurid meteor shower

Student teams may enter for $10, and adult teams cost $50. “Pickleball has taken Piedmont by storm, and we hope that this tournament is an opportunity to bring the community together and see which pair of players is the best,” said ASB president Jack Cramer. ASB will be accepting team registration up until Friday. “The amount of points to win and the length of each match will increase as each round goes on. It will be an elimination bracket tournament,” said Cramer. The action kicks off at 11:00 a.m. with the winners announced by 3:30 p.m. Spectators are encouraged to root for their favorite pickle paddlers. Food and baked goods will be available for purchase. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. articles.text: At Piedmont High’s Homecoming Rally on Friday, October 13, school pride bubbled and boiled over inside Binks Rawlings Gym. The inventiveness of students was on display as each grade battled in fun competitions, with students and staff decked out in Piedmont purple. The ASB school-wide event was hosted by student government leaders Phoenix Nwodeki, Jane Hempeck, and Sadie Town. The games and antics that played out on the basketball court included the likes of decathlon competition with the air of a cirque-du-soleil improv variety show. Peter Stokes was named Homecoming King and Beck Peterson as Homecoming Queen. The Junior Princesses on the Homecoming Court were Alina Shahid, and Ellie Bleharski. Millennium High homecoming court royalty included seniors Amiyah Denard and Lana Ivovich and 11th graders Shay Ottavino, and Keda King-Polk. Piedmont Police’s Juvenile Officer Hugo Diaz was invited to attend by Millenniumm High Principal Irma Nunez-Peters. It was the first school rally he has attended. “It’s really loud in here,“ Diaz said, “I’ve been to a bunch of football games, and this is louder,” he said. Piedmont students competed in innovative games, like sibling teams playing life-sized Hungry Hungry Hippos, with cardboard boxes for a mouth, a floor skate and colorful balloons. Student teams would push the other by their feet, like a wheelbarrow, while the “hippo” would try to “munch” the balloons. Students showed off their lung power, athletic prowess and creativity with an assortment of games on Friday afternoon. One class competition involved trash can targets, volleyballs and Connect Four. A well-rehearsed skit by memSiblings Charli (left) and Cash Panico in a new game called Hungry Hungry Hippos. Cash is trying to grab the balloons with the box. The second leg in a relay race had students dragged quickly across the court to the delight of the senior section. articles.text: Hollywood couldn’t write a better script. With just four seconds left in a 9-9 deadlocked Western Alameda County Conference battle between the Piedmont and Alameda boys’ water polo teams at Laney College on Thursday, October 12, the Highlanders called a timeout shortly after forcing a miss by the Hornets. From mid-pool, sophomore goalie Luke McAuliffe sent a high arching pass to Declan Linnane just a few feet in front of the Hornets’ goal. Reaching the ball at its peak, Linnane used his height and length to perfectly swat the ball into goal for a thrilling 10-9 victory. “At first I thought we might throw it up top and try to get a shot from the perimeter, but they were pressing us. Coach Rik told me to drive down and they will throw it over the top. Luke is one of the most accurate passers I’ve seen, so I knew it was coming. We only had a few seconds, so I had to go for the tap in,” said Linnane of the play. “Coach called a timeout Staff Photos Declan Linnane scored a dramatic tap-in shot at the last second of a 10-9 win over Alameda. and he said, ‘Luke, let it fly to Declan.’ I knew in my head Declan was going to make it. I was really nervous, but we did it. I was just thinking, loft it and make sure it’s above him,” mentioned McAuliffe. The play was called, “Storm The Castle.” It’s something they’ve only practiced on a limited scale. “We tried to get Declan in front of the cage and try to get a tip-ball. That was basically the play, when we saw the defender Coach Rik Krumins celebrates with Evan Dickason (left) and Gus von Metszch. Luke McAuliffe reaches for a save. He had the game-winning assist to Declan Linnane. come out and give Declan a path, I thought this might work,” said coach Rik Krumins. McAu l if fe’s pa ss wa s inch-perfect to where only Linnane could get a hand on it. Linnane, also a basketball player, resembled Lakers’ Hall of Famer Kareem Abdul-Jabbar landing a skyhook as he held off a defender. Piedmont looks ahead to the WACC Tournament at Encinal October 24-28, where they look to defend their league titles the last two years. articles.text: In spite of the score line, Piedmont’s 48-20 demolition of San Lorenzo last Saturday was not looking great. The Highlanders trailed 6-0 at the end of the first quarter. Apparently, coach Jordan Seiden chose to have a traditional halftime pep talk with his players well before halftime. The Highlanders went on to score 34 unanswered points before SLZ’s next touchdown which came near the end of the third quarter. PHS added 12 more points in the fourth. The win keeps Piedmont in contention for the WACC’s Shoreline Division title after Alameda lost to Arroyo. “It was a much-needed win, coming off a tough loss against Alameda. Seeing them lose to Arroyo gives us some life. We weren’t tackling well in the first quarter and weren’t blocking well. Once we got rolling and saw we could make some plays, we didn’t have any doubt,” said coach Seiden. It was another big day for receiver Sam Shelby, who had 11 pass receptions for 158 yards and two receiving touchdowns. He also had 68 rushing yards on three carries – two for touchdowns. His 55-yard touchdown run on an end-around boosted Piedmont’s lead to 34-6 with 4:17 left in the third quarter. “As a team, we played solid. We had a slow start but we started applying our offense as the game went on and ran things the way we needed to,” said Shelby. Shelby has been a catalyst in Piedmont’s breakout varsity season. He emerged as the team’s top receiver as a sophomore. He shows an innate ability to create deception e on the field by faking runs to the interior, only to break to the edge for long runs. It’s been a move Shelby has executed to perfection in several games. “It’s a credit to track. It’s really where I built up speed. I’m used on offense as a ‘sweep’ player, so I do my best to look for the outside,” said Shelby. Piedmont was without starting defensive end and left tackle Jordan Alemania, but filling in was senior Ben Breber. Appearing in only his third varsity football game, he impressed coach Seiden with his impact as a blocker and edge rusher. “Emmett Maxwell really encouraged me to come out and play. It’s my senior year so I thought I may as well play some Sam Shelby scored four touchdowns against San Lorenzo. Staff Photos football.” said Breber, a four-year tennis singles player. Game Recap Although Piedmont’s defense forced punts on San Lorenzo’s opening two possessions, the Highlanders committed turnovers and fumbles on their first two drives. The Grizzlies scored the game’s opening touchdown on a 51-yard broken play. With 1:35 left in the first period, Piedmont nearly scored on a 67-yard touchdown carry by Shelby on an end-around. The play was called back due to an illegal formation (no, not the A-11). Shelby then recorded three straight receptions before capping it off with a 25-yard reception into the end zone. Shelby kicked the extra point to make it 7-6 with 11:14 left in the second quarter. Piedmont forced a fumble on SLZ’s next possession where Brandon Dicke recovered at Piedmont’s 15-yard-line with 7:25 to go. From there, Piedmont drove 85 yards for a touchdown, sparked by a 30-yard touchdown by Albert Bellingrath, who shrugged off a tackle after catching a screen pass, making it 14-6 with 3:11 left. San Lorenzo’s next pass was intercepted by Miguel Long and returned to the 25-yard line with 1:44 remaining. PHS scored on four plays, including a seven-yard touchdown run by Shelby on another end-around with 36 seconds left for a 20-6 lead at halftime. Piedmont retained possession to start the third, and scored on a nineplay, 67-yard drive that featured a 25-yard touchdown catch by Shelby for a 27-6 lead with 7:57 left. Derek Schleuning forced a fumble on SLZ’s next drive, and the ball was recovered by recovered by Vince Arbit. On the next play, Shelby scored his 55-yard touchdown with 4:17 left in the third. Piedmont was rolling with a comfortable 34-6 lead. San Lorenzo got one back on its next drive, 34-12 after three minutes. Piedmont’s next score came from Cash Elmquist on a play-action pass for 23 yards in a 3rd-and-5 situation to boost its lead to 41-12. San Lorenzo scored with 4:46 left, 41-20, but Shelby responded with a 30-yard return to the Grizzlies’ 43, followed by a 20-yard run by quarterback Markos Lagios with 2:04 left. Final stats: Lagios completed 16-20 passes for 247 yards and four touchdowns, to go along with 48 rushing yards and a score. Shelby recorded 11 receptions for 158 yards and two receiving touchdowns, to go along with 68 rushing yards on three attempts for two rushing scores. Bellingrath had three receptions for 51 yards and a touchdown. Tommy Ashton had 45 yards on nine carries. articles.text: Piedmont suffered a pair of league losses over the past week. Staff Photos Piedmont High’s girls’ water polo team suffered a pair of losses against Western Alameda County Conference opponents last week, losing to Alameda 24-5 on Thursday, October 12, and 14-9 to American HS in Fremont the following day. Piedmont trailed American 4-2 to end the first quarter and 7-5 by halftime. Piedmont outscored the Eagles 4-2 in the third quarter to tie the match at 9-9 going into the fourth. However, American was able to score five unanswered goals in the fourth quarter. In the first quarter, American opened to a 3-0 advantage until Abigail Jacoby got PHS on the board with 3:32 on the clock. After an Eagles goal, Anne Reardon made it 4-2 with 56 seconds left. American extended the gap with a player advantage at 4:40, then Esme Krumins scored after 36 seconds. The Eagles scored on its next possession, but Reardon scored again, 6-4. On the last second of the half, Jacoby drew a 5-meter penalty, allowing Kat Melian to convert, 7-5 Eagles. Piedmont rallied for a 9-7 lead in the third quarter with goals by Sage Gilbert, Jacoby, and two by Melian with three minutes left. However, it marked the last time the Highlanders got on the scoreboard. American scored with a player-advantage before tying the game at 9-9 with 24 seconds left in the third quarter. In the fourth period, American took the lead after 30 seconds, then made it 11-9 after another minute. They added three more goals for the 14-9 victory. Final stats: Melian had three goals, Reardon had two goals and two steals, Jacoby scored twice, Gilbert had a goal and assist, Krumins had a goal and a steal. 24-5 loss to Alameda Alameda got out to an 8-2 lead to end the first quarter and extended the gap to 14-3 by halftime. The Hornets scored four times in the third quarter, while Piedmont put up two more goals in the fourth. Final stats: Melian scored three goals, while Vivian Burke and Gilbert had individual goals. articles.text: Piedmont High runners toed the line in a pair of meets over the past week, traveling to Woodward Park in Fresno for the Roughrider Invitational on Saturday, October 14. They earlier competed in a Western Alameda County Conference meet at Hayward High on Wednesday, October 11. At the Roughrider Invitational, Piedmont’s girls’ team placed fifth in a field of 23 schools. The boys’ team was sixth among 31 teams. For the league meet, Piedmont’s girls were fourth of eight and the boys placed fifth of 10. “We took them to Fresno for the Roughrider Invitational, giving the team a chance to get a taste of what it was like to run on the course where the state meet is held,” said coach Steve Zirkelbach. “The tenacity of the girls and their ability to run together as a group and not lose contact is one of the main reasons why they were able to do so well. The boys continue to run well, and Xander continues to shine as our top runner.” It was an impressive pair of races for senior Schulte-Sasse, a senior. He placed fifth of 277 at the Roughrider Invitational with a time of 16:22.84 on the State course. He was fourth out of 86 runners at the league meet in Hayward, site of the North Coast Section championship. He finished with an impressive time of 15:45.97. A four-year varsity runner, Schulte-Sasse has been on teams with some highly successful runners, notably Jack Stein (Class of 2022), Parker Terrill (Class of 2022), and Parker Long (Class of 2023). “Jack Stein was a really inclusive leader. I think he did a great job at keeping a level head, staySebastian Swain (right) and Julien Lee (left) sprint go the finish line. Xander Schulte-Sasse placed fifth at the Roughrider Invitational Meet at Woodward Park in Fresno. ing relaxed, and not stressing, but at the same time, he was ready to give his all when he needed. We’ve had some tremendous runners, I just want to remember the feeling of seeing them and how cool would it be to help build our runners like they did,” said Schulte-Sasse. On the girls’ team, sophomore Skylar Best and senior Jamie Schwarz have been leading the way. At the Roughrider Invitational, Schwarz was 15th of 202 in 20:27.60 and Best was two spots behind her in 17th at 20:36.48. In the WACC meet, Best was seventh of 64 with a time of 19:49.62 while Schwarz was 10th in 20:05.02. “I remember my freshman and sophomore year where we had a really small girls team. It’s really great to have new runners each year, everyone is super passionate and we have a tight-knit team,” said Schwarz. “Everyone has improved so much and it’s really great to see. Everyone is putting in a lot of work every day, so it’s really motivating to be on the team,” added Best. Roughrider Invitational Following Schwarz and Best, sophomore Cora Chun finished 49th of 212 with a time of 22:04.75. After her was freshman Leighton Mand in 53rd, clocking a 22:12.73. Freshman Gladwin Horsley rounded out PHS’ best five with a time of 22:37.01, finishing 63rd. articles.text: Berkeley Playhouse will premiere the musical Cinderella Enchanted, based on the 1997 movie of the same name, with performances shows opening November 3. The classic tale of Cinderella is reborn in this play with a Bay Area twist. Cinderella, played by Kennedy Joy Fullard, is a free-spirited Berkeley artist and Prince Christopher, played by Vinh G. Nguyen, is a wealthy Silicon Valley romantic. Prince Christopher hosts an extravagant ball where he meets Cinderella, only for her to leave the festivities before he can express his true feelings for her. Cinderella leaves behind nothing but a glass slipper which prompts the prince to embark on a mission to find the dainty shoe’s owner. Cinderella Enchanted is directed and choreographed by Khalia Davis. The director explained the significance of the mid-90’s film, and how it influenced Cinderella on stage. “[The 1997 movie] was really iconic and it set the bar for what is possible when you do musicals that are magical in that way,” Davis said. “[It was important that] audiences who are very familiar with that particular version see that reflected on the stage.” The Berkeley Playhouse production offers even more unique twists, she added. “I’m really excited that we get to honor and celebrate being able to see Prince Christopher’s life as well as Cinderella’s and the parallel life they are living. Cinderella is an aspiring writer who is fascinated by the world and Christopher is equally fascinated by the world but wants to know what he can do to make a positive impact outside of being born into royalty,” Davis said. Supporting cast members include Jennifer Marie Frazier as Fairy Godmother, Erika Coyne as Stepmother, Stephen Kanaski as Lionel as The Steward, Nicole Stanley as Queen Constantini and Kyle Herrera as King Maximillian. Cinderella Enchanted will be performed November 3 to December 22. Visit https://tickets.berkeleyplayhouse.org/Online/default.asp to purchase tickets. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum presents Inspiring Escapism: The Golden Gate International Exposition Interiors of Frances Elkins, a historian-led discussion, on Saturday, November 4. Visit the museum to hear historian Scott Powell discuss the career of interior designer Frances Adler Elkins, who worked primarily in California, Illinois and New York. Elkins is widely regarded as one of the most prominent and influential designers of the 20th century. She settled in Monterey and her first commissions were for residential designs for friends and social acquaintances. She later did important commercial work including hotels and retail stores. Elkins was known for her innovative style that drew from elements of both traditional and contemporary design. Her work continues to influence designers today. She worked alongside her brother, notable Chicago architect David Adler, on more than a dozen large homes throughout California, and in Chicago and New York. The presentation will show examples of Elkins’ work overall, Frances Elkins but will place particular emphasis on three buildings she decorated at the 1939-1940 Golden Gate Exposition on Yerba Buena Island – the Clubhouse, the San Francisco Building, and Hostess House. The exhibition includes rare images that will bring these interiors to life. The lecture begins at 10:30 a.m. The Treasure Island Museum is located on Treasure Island, at 1 Avenue of the Palms, #111. Visit https://www.eventbrite. c o m / e / i n s p i r i n g - e s c a p - ism-the-ggie-interiors-of-frances-elkins-tickets-735707991407 to purchase tickets.

articles.text: The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s first retrospective of Filipina artist Pacita Abad opens on October 21, and will be on view through January 28. Born in 1946 and raised in Basco, Philippines, she had a 32-year artistic career, creating a vast number of artworks that traverse a diversity of subjects, from colorful masks to underwater scenes to abstract compositions. The artist died in Singapore in 2004, but her colorful artwork uses a variety of mediums and reveals visual, material, and conceptual concerns that still resonate today. The SF MOMA exhibition features more than 40 pieces, including Abad’s signature trapunto paintings, which are stuffed, quilted canvases adorned with other raw, found Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/pacita-abad/ to learn more. articles.text: Visit Filoli Historic House and Gardens and tour the Gentleman’s Orchard, where you can enjoy fruit-picking and tasting, live music, and spiced cider made from the Filoli apple trees. The 6.8 acre Gentleman’s Orchard at Filoli preserves more than 600 apple, pear, plum, apricot, walnut, fig, and quince trees. While the estate Filoli is world-renowned for its flower beds, flora and fauna, the orchard has only been open to the public since 2021. “This orchard is about preserving this landscape feature of this estate. But through that we’re also trying to preserve some of the more rare heirloom varieties of fruit trees,” said lead horticulturist Jim Salyards. Much of the bounty will be gone by the end of autumn, but guests can pick and taste fruit off the trees and enjoy table grapes from the harvest. Other apples, pears, plums and apricots will be churned into butters or liquified into ciders, which guests can enjoy under the shade of Filoli’s walnut grove while younger guests build scarecrows. Admission includes access to the 54,000 square-foot Georgian mansion, and 16 acres of English Renaissance gardens. Orchard Days take place on Saturdays and Sundays through October 29. Filoli is located at 86 Cañada Road in Woodside, and is open every day from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. See https://filoli.org/ for tickets. Filoli Historic House & Gardens welcomes visitors this Autumn.

articles.text: Given what is unfolding in Israel and Gaza, Lemon Tree is an extraordinary must-see film. The question that Lemon Tree begs is, “can art, no matter how beautifully rendered, bridge a chasm of suspicion and enmity between two peoples who are locked in a kind of ritualistic Kabuki dance of violence devolved over decades?” Israeli director Eran Riklis has created a powerful metaphor in a lovely lemon grove that sits on the Palestinian side of the Green Line that separates Israel from the West Bank and the occupied territories. The grove – deeply green and dimpled by yellow lemons – is a startling contrast to the desiccated land that surrounds it. It is owned by Salma Zidane (Hiam Abbass), a Palestinian widow. The grove has been passed down from generation to generation. Always lovingly tended, it provides her with a meager income. Israeli defense minister, Israel Navon (Doron Tavory) and his lovely wife, Mira (Rona Lipaz-Michael), take up residence in a new home on the other side of the wire fence, in plain view of Salma as she waters the grove and picks the ripe lemons. Navon’s security forces conclude that the grove is a security threat, a possible sanctuary for terrorists wishing to launch attacks against the minister. They send Salma a letter informing her that the grove must be removed. Having the letter translated (she doesn’t read Hebrew), she makes a stunning decision: she will hire an attorney, Ziad Daud (Ali Suliman), and go to court to fight the decree. In a patriarchal culture, this is Tarik Kopty, Hiam Abbass, and Ali Suliman in Lemon Tree

articles.text: Super 8 is a great movie. What makes it great is the story, a solid coming of age tale of four boys and a girl, all on the cusp of adolescence, all set free from school, eager to begin their summer project: the shooting of a super 8 monster movie. On a balmy night, having sneaked out of their respective houses at midnight, they drive (don’t ask) to the local railroad station, and under a canopy of stars, the camera on a tripod, begin shooting their film. That is until they hear a train in the distance. Charley (Riley Griffith), the kid directing their movie, director, tells his crew to wait. He wants the train for background. And so the kids wait, the light of the train growing larger, the noise of the locomotive reaching them. And it’s at that moment something happens that sends the narrative in a profoundly different direction. It’s a huge shift, delivered with a riveting crash. articles.text: Come celebrate the 150th anniversary of Sergei Rachmaninoff at a concert on Saturday, October 21 at 4 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. The concert is presented by Early Childhood Mental Health Program (ECMHP) and will feature a presentation by psychiatrist Dr. Hunter Harris and performances by pianist Gwendolyn Mok and cellist Jerry Chang. ECMHP began as the Comprehensive Therapeutic Nursery School in 1974 as a grassroots effort led by a group of local parents, teachers, social workers, and community activists who were concerned about the number of children reaching kindergarten and struggling to benefit from education due to their adverse childhood experiences. The need was so great, and their success was so notable that, in a few years the program expanded and won government support to provide child-parent therapy and preschool mental health consultation services. ECMHP continues to pioneer programs that enhance the behavioral health by focusing on the relationship between caregivers and their children. Currently, ECMHP serves approximately 500 families. Additionally, ECMHP provides professional development opportunities and training for professionals working in mental health and early education.

articles.text: Part 2 in a series The list of Piedmont residents who have been employed at Pixar Studios includes Kiel Murray, who joined the studio in 2000 as a producer, screenwriter and Development Executive responsible for assisting directors in shaping stories. Partnering with her husband Phil Lorin, whom she met as undergraduate students at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, she scripted the first two Cars animated features for Pixar, and then working alone, she wrote Cars 3. She and Lorin went on to write and shoot two short films that were widely screened at festivals. While at Pixar, Murray also contributed to the story development and writing of acclaimed features such as Finding Nemo, Inside Out, Ratatouille, Brave, Raya and the Last Dragon, and Up. In 2019, Murray moved from Pixar to John Lasseter’s new venture, where she wrote the animated feature film Luck that began streaming on Apple tv in 2023. She is currently working on another project in development at Skydance Animation, the release date still to be determined. Murray grew up in Placerville and unlike most professional aniPiedmont filmmaker Kiel Murray maters and filmmakers, attended St. Mary’s College on a volleyball scholarship. The studied Communications and Theater, but it was in a fiction writing class where she discovered what would become a lifelong interest in writing for films and filmmaking. Looking beyond Pixar, it is impossible not to acknowledge Piedmont High School graduate Colin Trevorrow, a director, screenwriter, and filmmaker, best known for the compelling Jurassic franchise films. He graduated from New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts in 1999. As a teenager he won filmmaking awards from the Mill Valley Festival and the Sam Francisco Youth Film Festival. His first theatrical release was a 2004 documentary titled Reality Show. He went on to team up with NYU classmate Derek Connolly and co-wrote and directed the buddy cop feature called Cocked and Loaded. In 2012 he directed Safety Not Guaranteed. The film was nominated for the Independent Spirit Award for Best Feature Film, and was also nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Festival. Based on the film’s accolades, Trevorrow and Connolly were hired by Walt Disney Studio to write a script for the film, Flight of the Navigator. While busy writing directing and producing the Jurassic sequels, Trevorrow directed The Book of Henry, released in 2017, based on a story written by Greg Hurwitz. Reviews were mixed but it may be his best film, one that captures in a deeply moving way the essence of one family’s love and profound connection. In 2018, it was announced that Trevorrow would return to the Jurassic franchise and direct Jurassic World: World Dominion. This year he is slated to direct and produce the film Atlantis. He currently lives in the United Kingdom with his wife, Isabelle, and their two children. All of the above is testimony to the strong appeal of film and filmmaking.

The concert is presented by Early Childhood Mental Health Program (ECMHP) and will feature a presentation by psychiatrist Dr. Hunter Harris and performances by pianist Gwendolyn Mok and cellist Jerry Chang. ECMHP began as the Comprehensive Therapeutic Nursery School in 1974 as a grassroots effort led by a group of local parents, teachers, social workers, and community activists who were concerned about the number of children reaching kindergarten and struggling to benefit from education due to their adverse childhood experiences. The need was so great, and their success was so notable that, in a few years the program expanded and won government support to provide child-parent therapy and preschool mental health consultation services. ECMHP continues to pioneer programs that enhance the behavioral health by focusing on the relationship between caregivers and their children. Currently, ECMHP serves approximately 500 families. Additionally, ECMHP provides professional development opportunities and training for professionals working in mental health and early education. Piedmont – a surprising enclave for filmmakers By Chris Honoré Part 2 in a series The list of Piedmont residents who have been employed at Pixar Studios includes Kiel Murray, who joined the studio in 2000 as a producer, screenwriter and Development Executive responsible for assisting directors in shaping stories. Partnering with her husband Phil Lorin, whom she met as undergraduate students at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, she scripted the first two Cars animated features for Pixar, and then working alone, she wrote Cars 3. She and Lorin went on to write and shoot two short films that were widely screened at festivals. While at Pixar, Murray also contributed to the story development and writing of acclaimed features such as Finding Nemo, Inside Out, Ratatouille, Brave, Raya and the Last Dragon, and Up. In 2019, Murray moved from Pixar to John Lasseter’s new venture, where she wrote the animated feature film Luck that began streaming on Apple tv in 2023. She is currently working on another project in development at Skydance Animation, the release date still to be determined. Murray grew up in Placerville and unlike most professional aniPiedmont filmmaker Kiel Murray maters and filmmakers, attended St. Mary’s College on a volleyball scholarship. The studied Communications and Theater, but it was in a fiction writing class where she discovered what would become a lifelong interest in writing for films and filmmaking. Looking beyond Pixar, it is impossible not to acknowledge Piedmont High School graduate Colin Trevorrow, a director, screenwriter, and filmmaker, best known for the compelling Jurassic franchise films. He graduated from New York University’s Tisch School of the Arts in 1999. As a teenager he won filmmaking awards from the Mill Valley Festival and the Sam Francisco Youth Film Festival. His first theatrical release was a 2004 documentary titled Reality Show. He went on to team up with NYU classmate Derek Connolly and co-wrote and directed the buddy cop feature called Cocked and Loaded. In 2012 he directed Safety Not Guaranteed. The film was nominated for the Independent Spirit Award for Best Feature Film, and was also nominated for the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Festival. Based on the film’s accolades, Trevorrow and Connolly were hired by Walt Disney Studio to write a script for the film, Flight of the Navigator. While busy writing directing and producing the Jurassic sequels, Trevorrow directed The Book of Henry, released in 2017, based on a story written by Greg Hurwitz. Reviews were mixed but it may be his best film, one that captures in a deeply moving way the essence of one family’s love and profound connection. In 2018, it was announced that Trevorrow would return to the Jurassic franchise and direct Jurassic World: World Dominion. This year he is slated to direct and produce the film Atlantis. He currently lives in the United Kingdom with his wife, Isabelle, and their two children. All of the above is testimony to the strong appeal of film and filmmaking. It is a one and half story Craftsman style home with wide eaves and exposed rafter ends that were typical of this style. The Schmidts were married in 1908 and lived in the house until the 1940s. The walkers then went down El Cerrito to Witter Field to see the work being done. Drainage trenches and pipes were being laid, and there were large mounds of dirt in the center of the field. According to a story in last week’s Piedmont Post, completion of the project has been delayed until January primarily because of work to be done by EBMUD. The Witter Field site has its own history. Land developer Frank C. Havens created Piedmont Park in 1898 as a way to draw visitors and future residents to Piedmont. The main entrance to the park was at the current bus stop across from the Wells Fargo bank on Highland Avenue. Visitors could also enter the park on a path from Grand Avenue on what is now Palm Drive. Havens also creates a large circular maze of hedges as an attraction in the natural bowl where Witter Field stands today. Havens lined the lane to the “Maze” with palm trees. Some of them still survive on Palm Drive. These majestic palms are over 125 years old and are the last remaining ones. One block later on Park View Avenue they saw a home with very large black spiders all over its exterior and a long line of crows along its roof line ready for Halloween. Then it was down the length of Palm Drive to Wildwood Avenue Along the way they couldn’t resist climbing a newly discovered alley road to Warfield Avenue, and then to Winsor and Wildwood Avenues. On Wildwood, neighbors Nadine Guffanti and Sarah Johnson told the group the history of the house between theirs. A woman built the house in 1927 and lived in it for 30 years. Later her daughter and granddaughter lived there. After the granddaughter died, it was vacant for many years until some squatters took up residence with the intent of living in it long enough to claim it. They were discovered and removed. The walkers made their way back to the Exedra via Piedmont Park. articles.text: A 1906 scandal that riveted America resulted in two classic works of art: Theodore Dreiser’s 1925 novel, An American Tragedy, based on the lurid 1906 events, and 1951’s Hollywood version of the book, A Place in the Sun. A lucky Piedmont audience had a chance to check out the 1951 movie at last Thursday’s 10th iteration of the Second Thursday Film Fest. Audience members were treated to intense drama and romance. The film is an example of old-style filmmaking at its best, featuring taut storytelling, meticulous visual design, stunning black-and-white cinematography, and glamorous stars in the persons of Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift, with Shelley Winters making the third in a doomed love triangle. The central character is poor but eager young George Eastman (Clift), who arrives in town hoping to take advantage of a promise his wealthy industrialist uncle made to help him out. His reward is, at first, a low-level job in the Eastman swim suit factory, where he begins to romance a naive factory girl named Alice Tripp (Winters). When the wealthy Eastmans begin to notice George and set in motion plans to move him up in the business hierarchy, things begin to go wrong rather than right. He’s invited to an elegant social event, at which he meets beautiful and wealthy Angela Vickers (Taylor). They fall in love, but what’s George to do about Alice Tripp? She’s pregnant, it turns out, and she demands that he marry her. One thing he does, knowing she can’t swim, is row her out to the middle of a lonely lake. Charlie Chaplin called A Place in the Sun the best movie about America ever made. Directed by George Stevens, it was nominated for 9 Academy Awards and won six. The Piedmont film group’s post-showing discussion produced enthusiastic thumbs-up reactions, with praise for the actors, the suspense, and the drama. The Piedmont Film Fest’s next offering, on November 9, is the Italian comedy/drama, Life Is Beautiful, made in 1997 and starring Roberto Begnini, who earned a best actor Academy Award for his role. Successfully shown world-wide, it won the 1998 Cannes Grand Prix. Sponsored by the Rec Department, the Film Fest takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a showtime at 10:30. The event is free and open to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration with the PRD is required at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. You’re welcome to bring snacks or lunch.

articles.text: Caroline Hutchnecker Peters, born to Holocaust Survivors on May 20, 1949, touched the lives of many with her boundless love, joyful spirit, and her unmistakable curly hair that could brighten even the cloudiest of days. She passed away September 7, 2023, leaving behind a legacy of laughter, love, and cherished memories. In the early days in Piedmont, Caroline was a vibrant force on the tennis courts. Piedmont Pool held a special place in her heart, where she later exercised, spending countless hours swimming laps and sharing smiles and laughter with friends and family. But perhaps what her friends will remember the most is her infectious giggles that could fill a room with happiness. Her laughter was a testament to her zest for life and her ability to find joy in the simplest of moments. Caroline is survived by her beloved family – her devoted husband Ronny Peters, her daughters Rebecca Triki and husband Cherif Triki, and Michelle McGilloway and husband Shane McGilloway. She is also survived by her son Jeff Peters and his wife Bailey Peters. Caroline was not only a loving mother and wife, but also a cherished grandmother (Bubba) to her five wonderful grandchildren, Adam, Logan, Liam, Tahlia and Brody. Caroline’s love and warmth extended to her family, and her legacy will continue through the bonds she created and the values she instilled in her children and grandchildren. May Caroline’s memory continue to shine brightly through the lives of her husband, children, and grandchildren. articles.text: Jason Darling of El Sobrante passed away unexpectedly at home in the early morning of Saturday, September 30, 2023, at the age of 50. Born Jason Allen Darling on November 13, 1972 in Oakland, Jason was the son of Diane Cameron Mockel and the late Kenneth Allen Darling. He was raised by his grandparents, Marilyn and Bud Miller, and then by his mother Diane and stepfather Kenneth Mockel of Piedmont. He attended Beach Elementary School and graduated from Piedmont High in 1991. Always full of life and boundless energy, Jason started doing voices and celebrity impersonations at a young age, constantly fooling his grandparents with prank phone calls. More than anything Jason loved to make people laugh. Jason became a big brother at age 10, when Diane and Ken’s second son, Jamieson “Jamie” Mockel, was born. Jason and Jamie became incredibly close over the years, In 2009, while living in Pinole, Jason met the love of his life, Kristen Hamlett, who was drawn to Jason’s irreverent sense of humor and ceaseless jokes. They were married on May 17, 2012. Jason was a loving husband and a devoted father. Jason was a lifelong technophile. At age 11 his uncle, Dennis Mockel, built him a high-powered i486 PC. Around 2014, following urging by his uncle Ron Mockel of the Piedmont Adult School, Jason returned to Piedmont School District as District IT Specialist II. Jason’s years of experience were instrumental in PUSD’s launch of the Connected Learning Chromebook 1:1 program and the technology infrastructure in the STEAM and Theater buildings. He loved his work and encouraged his brother Jamie to come work for PUSD as an English teacher and the two loved working together at their alma mater. Jason’s co-workers recall his boundless positivity and willingness to go the extra mile to help with any project, approaching every task with kindness and patience, even when dealing with the challenging nature of IT issues. Jason’s love of Piedmont also ran deep. After graduating from Piedmont High he became a paraeducator at the middle school and high school. He worked at Piedmont Adult School, along with his grandmother Peggy Mockel. He was also an intrepid world traveler, taking countless cruises over the years with his family, especially his uncle and constant companion, Ron. His travels included Central and South America, the Caribbean, Canada, and Alaska, and he loved to entertain fellow passengers at comedy open mics and with his karaoke skills. Jason is survived by his wife Kristen, son Jayden, daughter Jasmine, and three dogs, Dexter, Dorie, and Fonzie. He is also survived by his mother and father, Diane and Ken, brother Jamie, sibling-in-law Cassidy Williams, and the entire Darling, Mockel, and Hamlett families. articles.text: On September 22, eight members of the Piedmont Seniors group visited the facilities of Canine Companions, a 14-acre campus located in Santa Rosa. The Seniors toured the facilities with a personal guide. There are several categories of dog companions: service dogs, who assist their owners with various tasks; dogs for disabled owners who require more than simple tasks, such as opening doors; and dogs for veterans who have PTSD. Clients range in age from five years old to senior citizens, and they are eligible as long as they can properly handle the dog. The Canine Companion organization has its own breeding facilities to ensure that puppies are afforded the best quality of training. Breeders stay on campus for about three weeks and puppies start their training at about six months. Golden retrievers and Labrador retrievers are the most common service dogs. Trainers are usually located within 90 miles of the main facility. If dogs don’t graduate from the training program, most of them are usually adopted by the trainers. Those interested in raising and training a service puppy may contact the Canine Companion website. Canine Companions has been in business for over 40 years. At the grand opening in 1996, Charles Schulz chiseled his Peanuts character into the concrete at the Santa Rosa headquarters. There are five additional locations throughout the U.S. The working life of a service dog is eight to 10 years. At the headquarters, there’s a veterinarian clinic with records of all dogs that have graduated. There is also a puppy park where the puppies meet their trainers; a grooming room where the dogs get bathed; and a supply room where the food is kept and distributed. The dogs are fed dry food only twice a day, and puppies get food three times per day. One of the ways that keeps the air fresh is by planting roses and citrus trees throughout the compound. The main lawn area was landscaped by master gardeners. The facilities have a trainers’ building that houses up to 10 trainers along with their dogs. Each trainer has a fully furnished room with a handicapped accessible private bathroom. There is a community kitchen and huge common area for socializing. There are also ‘trade’ clothing and dog toys for trainers to either donate or take.Canine Companions is primarily funded through grants and donations and has a mostly volunteer staff. Many of whom have been helping for years. Graton Resort and Casino, which began as a casino, now boasts a luxurious hotel, spa, swimming pool and entertainment venue, along with a variety of fine restaurants, and a food court. Dear MacMama: I have very poor eyesight and am wondering if there is a way to make things easier to see on my Mac. Lynde, Oakland Dear Lynde: This is an excellent question! Many people don’t know that most computers, including Apple, have many ways to compensate for vision, hearing, and even touch. This is under the system preference pane, “Accessibility”. Here are some of the options that allow for help on your Mac if you have poor vision, hearing or difficulty with hand movements. There are separate settings for Vision, Hearing, Motor, and General. • Vision: Voice over, Zoom, Display, Spoken Content, Descriptions. Voice Over is a screen reader, and allows people with vision issues, and even blindness to navigate through voice prompts. For example, if you move through the dock, the voice will say “Mail, Safari, Pages” as you pass those with your cursor. You can also customize this and train this feature to recognize certain words and speed up or slow down the talk speed. Zoom, is just what it sounds like. It all allows you to zoom in full screen, or picture in picture and more through the use of modifier keys (like option or control). One feature in the zoom section is “Hover Text”. If you turn this on and hold down the command button, as you hover your cursor over text, it will show a larger version of that text. Display allows you to increase contrast, make the text bigger, changing size and color and size of the cursor, etc. Spoken Content allows you to customize the sound and speaking rate of the system voice, and determine what it tells you. Descriptions allows you to have audio descriptions for visual content in media. • Hearing: Audio, RTT, Captions. Audio does not have a lot of features, just allowing for the screen to flash if an alert comes in. RTT (real time text) allows for calls to deaf users that use a TDD device. Captions allow users to customize system wide captions. • Motor: Voice Control, Keyboard, Pointer Control

articles.text: Protecting elderly loved ones from falls Bathrooms can be a perilous place in the house, especially for people who are older or living with a chronic condition that can make falls more likely. Much like the kitchen, the bathroom is a risky space in the home with hazards such as slippery surfaces and sharp objects. One study found that the most common location for fall injuries in the home was the bathroom, including when people are hurrying to the bathroom. A National Institute on Aging statistic states that 80% of falls in the home happen in the bathroom. Yet, these injuries are not just the result of missing grab bars in the shower and not all of the risk involves a fall. Consider the following risk factors that could lead to your elderly loved one injuring themselves in the bathroom: 1) Bathmat in the tub or shower In theory, these mats are there to prevent a fall on the slick surface. In reality, they can become a tripping hazard as they bunch up or move when stepped on. The solution is to attach non-slip decals to the surface of the tub or shower. 2) Lack of adequate lighting It’s not uncommon for people aged 65 or older, or those living with certain conditions or taking specific medications, to need to use the restroom in the middle of the night. Unfortunately, being half awake is only going to increase the chances of tripping or slipping and possibly falling in the bathroom. The solution is to install a simple night light that can at the very least make it clear where the light switch is in the dark. 3) No handheld showerhead When someone needs to use a chair in the shower or tub, they will also need an easy-to-reach shower head that they can move around without too much twisting and turning. The solution to this potential bathroom hazard is to add an adjustable shower head that allows the individual to clean themselves while remaining safely seated. 4) Hot water As we age, our skin becomes thinner and more sensitive to exposure to high water temperatures. At the same time, there is a decreased ability to sense when water is so hot it can scald or burn the skin. Help prevent burn injuries to your elderly loved one by having a professional handyman set the water heater thermostat between 110 to 120 degrees, which is considered safe by experts. Learn more about helping the elderly stay healthy and safe at home by contacting our office or consulting with a Certified Senior Advisor (https://www.csa.us/). Homewatch CareGivers is locat­ ed at 3820 Broadway in Oakland and is owned and operated by Piedmon­ ters Benjamin and Leah Bloom. You can reach them at 835-9362 or find them at www.CarePiedmont.com. and Switch Control. Voice Control allows users to control their Macs with just their voice. You can choose and customize commands for this feature. Keyboard has several features that allows users to configure the behavior of the keyboard. You can enable “sticky keys” for those that cannot hold keys down for shortcuts, customize the pointer (cursor). With Pointer users can enable the powerful “Alternate Control Methods”. With this feature, a user who does not have reliable use of their hands can use their head and even facial expressions to control the pointer. Switch Control allows users to operate their Macs with external buttons or “switches”, which Apple has for sale on their website. • General: Siri and Accessibility Shortcut. Siri allows users to use keyboards to type commands to Siri, which is useful for those who are deaf or have speech difficulty. Shortcut allows a user to get an Accessibility pop up menu using a keyboard shortcut (Option-Command-F5 is the default, but that also is customizable). Most of these features are also available on the iPhone, iPad and even Apple TV. Apple is committed to making sure that users of all physical, hearing, and visual capabilities can use their devices with ease. There are many more ways to customize all these features, from making the text larger on your system, to using voice over, to making your pointer larger with a customizable outline color. It’s comforting to know that if you can’t use your Mac, with the default settings, they can be customized to your comfort level. The solution is to install a simple night light that can at the very least make it clear where the light switch is in the dark. 3) No handheld showerhead When someone needs to use a chair in the shower or tub, they will also need an easy-to-reach shower head that they can move around without too much twisting and turning. The solution to this potential bathroom hazard is to add an adjustable shower head that allows the individual to clean themselves while remaining safely seated. 4) Hot water As we age, our skin becomes thinner and more sensitive to exposure to high water temperatures. At the same time, there is a decreased ability to sense when water is so hot it can scald or burn the skin. Help prevent burn injuries to your elderly loved one by having a professional handyman set the water heater thermostat between 110 to 120 degrees, which is considered safe by experts. Learn more about helping the elderly stay healthy and safe at home by contacting our office or consulting with a Certified Senior Advisor (https://www.csa.us/). READ IT IN THE POST Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama: I have very poor eyesight and am wondering if there is a way to make things easier to see on my Mac. Lynde, Oakland Dear Lynde: This is an excellent question! Many people don’t know that most computers, including Apple, have many ways to compensate for vision, hearing, and even touch. This is under the system preference pane, “Accessibility”. Here are some of the options that allow for help on your Mac if you have poor vision, hearing or difficulty with hand movements. There are separate settings for Vision, Hearing, Motor, and General. • Vision: Voice over, Zoom, Display, Spoken Content, Descriptions. Voice Over is a screen reader, and allows people with vision issues, and even blindness to navigate through voice prompts. For example, if you move through the dock, the voice will say “Mail, Safari, Pages” as you pass those with your cursor. You can also customize this and train this feature to recognize certain words and speed up or slow down the talk speed. Zoom, is just what it sounds like. It all allows you to zoom in full screen, or picture in picture and more through the use of modifier keys (like option or control). One feature in the zoom section is “Hover Text”. If you turn this on and hold down the command button, as you hover your cursor over text, it will show a larger version of that text. Display allows you to increase contrast, make the text bigger, changing size and color and size of the cursor, etc. Spoken Content allows you to customize the sound and speaking rate of the system voice, and determine what it tells you. Descriptions allows you to have audio descriptions for visual content in media. • Hearing: Audio, RTT, Captions. Audio does not have a lot of features, just allowing for the screen to flash if an alert comes in. RTT (real time text) allows for calls to deaf users that use a TDD device. Captions allow users to customize system wide captions. • Motor: Voice Control, Keyboard, Pointer Control and Switch Control. Voice Control allows users to control their Macs with just their voice. You can choose and customize commands for this feature. Keyboard has several features that allows users to configure the behavior of the keyboard. You can enable “sticky keys” for those that cannot hold keys down for shortcuts, customize the pointer (cursor). With Pointer users can enable the powerful “Alternate Control Methods”. With this feature, a user who does not have reliable use of their hands can use their head and even facial expressions to control the pointer. Switch Control allows users to operate their Macs with external buttons or “switches”, which Apple has for sale on their website. • General: Siri and Accessibility Shortcut. Siri allows users to use keyboards to type commands to Siri, which is useful for those who are deaf or have speech difficulty. Shortcut allows a user to get an Accessibility pop up menu using a keyboard shortcut (Option-Command-F5 is the default, but that also is customizable). Most of these features are also available on the iPhone, iPad and even Apple TV. Apple is committed to making sure that users of all physical, hearing, and visual capabilities can use their devices with ease. There are many more ways to customize all these features, from making the text larger on your system, to using voice over, to making your pointer larger with a customizable outline color. It’s comforting to know that if you can’t use your Mac, with the default settings, they can be customized to your comfort level. articles.text: This year’s Pumpkin Festival at Mountain View Cemetery marks the return of the cemetery’s most popular After an absence of four years due to COVID and post-COVID, Mountain View Cemetery will host the 15th Annual Pumpkin Festival on Saturday, October 28, at noon. Community members and children are invited to Mountain View Cemetery’s pumpkin patch in the main meadow just inside the main gates for a fun-filled day of free Halloween events. There will be inflatable bounce houses, face painting, clown balloon artists, and a craft area where kids can decorate costumes, masks, treat bags, and pumpkins. Young children will be able to pick up one free pumpkin per child in person at the information booth while supplies last. The entertainment company Furs, Scales & Tails will also have a live animal show for kids at the festival. Former kindergarten teacher Tracy Hill has been performing shows in Northern California for 15 years. Hill’s shows have been known to include baby chicks, hamsters, guinea pigs, rabbits, turtles, snakes, ducks, tortoises, lizards, tarantulas, roosters, giant millipedes, frogs, chickens, and even hairless rats. Food truck vendors will also be on-site to sell tacos, empanadas, lumpia, burgers, fries, hot dogs, hot links, Italian ice, and more. The 15th Annual Pumpkin Festival will take place following the Piedmont Avenue Halloween parade. Admission is free. Parents must accompany their children to this event. Mountain View Cemetery is located at 5000 Piedmont Avenue in Oakland. A live animal show for kids was part of Mountain View Cemetery’s 2019 Pumpkin Festival.
